alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different verse (Mark 9:4, the appearance of Elijah and Moses), while the Greek and Peshitta attest Mark 9:3 (the transfiguration of Jesus' garments). This represents a complete textual displacement, likely a scribal error in the Vulgate manuscript tradition or a misalignment in the source data.

Greek uses the article + plural noun + possessive pronoun (τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ, 'his garments'); Peshitta employs a singular construct form with pronominal suffix (ܠܒܘܫܗ, 'his garment'), a typical Syriac idiom treating collective clothing as a singular mass noun.

Greek places the verb ἐγένετο ('became') before the participle; Peshitta places the copula ܗܘܐ after the initial participle ܘܡܙܗܪ ('and shining'); Vulgate erant follows the participle loquentes in the displaced verse 4 text.

Greek uses a present participle + adjective + adverb construction (στίλβοντα λευκὰ λίαν, 'shining, exceedingly white'); Peshitta employs two coordinated finite verbs with an adverb (ܘܡܙܗܪ... ܘܡܚܘܪ ܛܒ, 'and it shone... and [was] very white'), reflecting Syriac preference for paratactic verbal chains over participial modification.

Greek οἷα ('such as') introduces a relative comparison; Peshitta ܐܝܟܢܐ ('as, in such manner') serves the same comparative function but with a slightly different semantic nuance, emphasizing manner rather than quality.

Greek γναφεὺς ('launderer, fuller') is a technical term for a professional cloth-bleacher; Peshitta substitutes ܕܒܢܝ ܐܢܫܐ ('sons of men, human beings'), generalizing the comparison from a specific trade to humanity in general, thereby intensifying the supernatural quality of the whiteness.

Greek δύναται is third-person singular ('is able'); Peshitta ܡܫܟܚܝܢ is third-person plural ('are able'), agreeing with the plural subject ܕܒܢܝ ܐܢܫܐ ('sons of men'), whereas Greek's singular verb agrees with the singular γναφεύς.

Greek uses adverb + infinitive (οὕτως λευκᾶναι, 'thus to whiten'); Peshitta employs the prefixed infinitive ܠܡܚܘܪܘ ('to whiten') without an explicit adverb of manner, the manner being implied by the preceding context.
Vulgate loquentes cum Jesu ('speaking with Jesus') belongs to the displaced verse 4 and has no correspondence in the Greek or Peshitta witnesses of verse 3.
